extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for applying and assessing inductive inferences: how to apply approximate generalizations to particulars, how to combine such generalizations probabilistically, when approximations may be treated as universals, and how existence, resemblance, and mathematical axioms function in inductive logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply approximate generalizations only within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposition 'Most A are B' has been established by sufficient induction, we may conclude that any particular A is B with a probability proportioned to the preponderance of affirmative instances over exceptions, but only within the limits of time, place, and circumstance embraced in the observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not project averages beyond the contexts in which they were observed. Numerical precision in conclusions is only warranted when the underlying data admit numerical precision. Averages are of little use for particular individual cases outside the sampled conditions (example: life-tables useful to insurance offices, but not definitive for an individual's life). Treat general averages as first approximations; refine by assessing particular circumstances of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying genus averages to known subclasses or special circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: If we know of a particular instance not only that it falls under A, but to what species or variety of A it belongs, we shall generally err in applying to that instance the average struck for the whole genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the particular belongs to a subclass or is under a particular set of circumstances not represented in the overall average, use the species-specific average or adjust the inference accordingly. Anti-pattern: assuming the genus-average applies uniformly across heterogeneous subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine independent generalizations by 'addition' to increase probability
rubrics_metrics.description: When each of two approximate generalizations is separately applicable to the case, combining them (addition) yields a probability greater than either alone (e.g., Most A are B; Most C are B; this thing is both A and C; therefore it is probably B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute combined probability only under an independence assumption; the example shows combining fractions to find a higher joint probability (worked example: two-thirds and three-quarters -> 11/12). Use this when premises are unconnected witnesses or unconnected attributes corroborating the same conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require independence when multiplying probabilities from separate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: In combining probabilities (e.g., chance that A is not B times chance that C is not B), it is supposed that the probabilities arising from A and C are independent of each other; there must not be such connection that belonging to one class increases chance of belonging to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A and C are correlated (e.g., not-Bs that are Cs largely overlap with not-Bs that are As), then the product rule and the inference of increased probability are invalid; the combined probability may not improve over the single source. Check for overlaps/causal links before applying multiplicative combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that chain (deductive) combination diminishes probability
rubrics_metrics.description: When only one proposition is directly applicable and the second applies only by virtue of the first (Most A are B; Most B are C; this is a C; therefore it is probably A then B), each deduction step generally reduces the degree of probability of the final conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chain of reasoning through multiple approximate generalizations progressively dwindles the probability (errors aggregate). Unless premises are very nearly universal (close to certainty), a few steps can render the conclusion worthless. Anti-pattern: relying on 'hearsay of a hearsay' or marks of marks without accounting for diminishing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure aggregate error multiplicatively when chaining near-universal premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If premises are nearly universal (e.g., nine-tenths, eight-ninths, seven-eighths), the proportion of A which are D after chaining equals the product of the proportions (e.g., 9/10 * 8/9 * 7/8 = 7/10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When numerical estimates exist for each premise and premises are fairly distributed with respect to one another, compute the aggregate probability by multiplying the relevant proportions. Use this to quantify how error accumulates across steps; remember such computation presupposes fair distribution and no hidden concentration of exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform approximate generalizations into universals with explicit provisos when exceptions are identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason for stopping at an approximate generalization is inconvenience rather than impossibility, and we know the character distinguishing exceptions, we may substitute a universal proposition with a proviso (e.g., 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making exceptions explicit as conditions, the proposition can be treated as universal for ratiocination, and the provisos can be carried forward to the conclusion to account for aggregate error. This preserves trackability of errors when chaining many propositions. Use when exception-causing traits are known and describable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat approximate generalizations as universal for inquiries about masses
rubrics_metrics.description: In political or social inquiries concerning the actions of multitudes, it is generally enough to know that most persons act in a particular way; what is true approximately of individuals is true absolutely of masses for the purposes of statesmanship and collective arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For policy and collective predictions, approximate truths about most individuals can be treated as effectively universal because aggregate behavior is determined by the majority. Use approximate generalizations confidently when the subject-matter is large-scale social phenomena and outcomes depend on majorities rather than single peculiar individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer existence of unperceived phenomena from inductive laws of succession or co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a phenomenon, when not directly perceived, is inferred from some inductive law of succession or co-existence; we prove the existence of a thing by proving that it is connected by succession or co-existence with some known thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed uniformities of succession/co-existence as evidential marks for inferring existence beyond direct perception. This aligns existence-inference with the same inductive principles used for temporal/causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that a single positive instance can establish a general existence claim
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions affirming bare existence are sufficiently proved by a single instance (e.g., if it could be ascertained positively that sea-serpents or unicorns had been seen even once, their existence would be established).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence-generalizations differ from statistical generalizations: one well-attested instance can establish that something can occur. Scrutinize the reliability of the single instance, but do not demand many examples for bare existence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare resemblances directly when possible; otherwise compare via a third object
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance is ultimately settled by direct juxtaposition, but when direct comparison is impracticable, compare each object with a third object that can be transported between them and use general propositions (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct, part-by-part comparisons whenever feasible. When impossible, employ transitive principles and auxiliary standards to infer resemblance. Anti-pattern: assuming surface similarity without adequate part-wise comparison or suitable intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical laws of resemblance from causal-derived resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical resemblances (axioms of equality, inequality, proportionality) are true irrespective of causal origin, while many empirical resemblances (e.g., equality of areas in orbital motion) are derived from laws of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about resemblance, identify whether the claimed resemblance is a purely mathematical truth (independent of physical cause) or an empirical regularity that depends on causal laws. This affects what kind of inductive support and generality is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge mathematical axioms as inductive truths from perpetual perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The axioms of mathematics (e.g., 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another') are inductive truths resting on perpetual observation and never having been found false; their evidence is akin to that for universal causal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mathematical axioms as foundational inductive premises justified by continuous successful perception. Use them as secure bases for deductive systems, but recognize their empirical origin in repeated verification rather than metaphysical intuition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand number-names as connoting physical modes of formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of numbers denote physical phenomena and connote the characteristic manner in which aggregates are formed and may be separated into parts; arithmetical propositions assert modes of formation of given numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing arithmetic in inductive arguments, be aware that numerical terms ultimately reference tangible aggregation operations. This grounds arithmetic's inductive status and explains how mathematical reasoning connects with empirical construction and measurement.
